transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-04
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Asha (CTO - Penumbra), Leo (ML Eng), Jordan (Infra Lead)
Links referenced: Pricing deck (redwood.com/deck/dedicated-pricing), Burst playbook (redwood.com/playbooks/burst), Benchmark sheet (sheets.link/penumbra-bench)

Summary:
Penumbra is evaluating Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private; primary need is predictable capacity for customer-facing chat inference with occasional large surge events (marketing drops). They need tenant isolation, bring-your-own-key KMS, SOC2 evidence and detailed burst guardrails.

Topics covered:
- Current infra and what 'reserved' means
- Burst strategy and fallback to hosted
- Isolation: node-level tenancy, VPC, data in flight/at rest
- Prewarm/warm-pool strategies and billing implications
- Sizing: tokens per request, concurrency, models (70B-ish), and expected QPS
- Compliance: SSO, KMS, audit logs, data retention

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros? I'll start, Maya Thompson, AE at Redwood, Carlos Ruiz, our SE is with me.
[00:12] Asha: Hi, Asha here, CTO at Penumbra. Leo, Jordan are with me. We're excited but have a bunch of constraints.
[00:20] Leo: Hey, Leo, ML. We've been running a homegrown endpoint for RTP chat, hitting latency pains during spikes.
[00:28] Jordan: Jordan, infra. We operate in GCP, have strict VPC peering and KMS policies.
[00:35] Maya: Great. Goal for today: understand your workload, isolation needs, and whether Dedicated reserved GPUs make sense. We'll surface tradeoffs — latency, cost, and operational complexity.
[00:45] Carlos: Quick Q to ground us: what's a typical request in tokens, and what's peak concurrent users you've seen?
[00:53] Asha: Average turn is 220 tokens, peaks up to 1.2k tokens on long context. Concurrent active users around 350 normally, but we've seen marketing-driven spikes to ~3k concurrent in 10–15 minute windows.
[01:10] Leo: To add, those spikes last 5–20 minutes; then drop back. We also do batch embedding jobs overnight, separate pools maybe.
[01:20] Carlos: Okay that helps. So two workloads: steady low-latency chat and periodic high-throughput spikes. Redwoods' Dedicated can reserve nodes and configure prewarm/warm pools to reduce cold-starts.
[01:33] Asha: And the fallback story? If we reserve but there's an unexpected higher surge, can we burst to hosted? We need to guarantee user experience.
[01:41] Maya: Yes, we do hybrid routing. Policy-based routing can send overflow to Hosted models with throttles and circuit-breakers. There are trade-offs: hosted variants might be lower-cost but have slightly different latency and different SLA.
[01:52] Jordan: Is there any data separation issue when bursting to Hosted? We need to ensure no customer PII leaves our VPC; default policy is data must not go to managed endpoints.
[02:02] Carlos: We can set routing to only send anonymized or hashed payloads to Hosted, or use a fallback model that's trained on public data only. For regulated traffic, customers often prefer private/on-prem route for those requests.
[02:15] Asha: So for our main chat, we can't send raw messages out of our VPC. We could accept fallback only for non-PII or to return a degraded response. Is there a way to precompute fallbacks?
[02:25] Maya: Absolutely. Common pattern: set policy to serve core requests on Dedicated; on overflow return a cached generic response or route to a hosted-safe model after stripping PHI. We also support configurable token redaction rules.
[02:37] Leo: About isolation — we need node-level fencing so that other tenants can't noisy-neighbor on our reserved GPUs. How granular is that?
[02:45] Carlos: Dedicated offers tenant-isolated pools: either whole-node reservation or soft-isolation with cgroup-level scheduling. For strict isolation, whole-node pinned allocation is best — it's more expensive but gives predictable performance.
[02:58] Jordan: Do you support our KMS? We use a customer-managed key (Cloud KMS) with HSM-backed keys.
[03:05] Maya: Yes, for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. For Redwood Dedicated (managed), we offer BYOK for an enterprise plan and can discuss HSM integration on the contract.
[03:16] Asha: SOC2 reports and audit logs — how detailed are the logs? We need event-level logs for token access and admin actions.
[03:24] Carlos: Console provides audit trails, token-level cost/latency, and per-route logging. For enterprise, we can increase retention and push logs to your SIEM via secure endpoints.
[03:35] Leo: SSO — SAML support for RBAC? We need SCIM provisioning.
[03:39] Maya: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported. RBAC roles can be synced to your identity provider.
[03:46] Jordan: Ok good. Now sizing: given 70B-ish model, 220 tokens average, 350 steady conc, peaks 3k — what's your recommended reserved pool size?
[03:58] Carlos: Rough calc: depends on model throughput on chosen hardware. For example, on H100-class nodes with quantized 8-bit runtimes, a node might support ~120 concurrent low-latency streams at 8–12 tokens/sec per stream. For 350 steady conc you'd want ~3 nodes to 4 nodes; for peak 3k you'd rely on warm pool + burst to hosted or prewarm additional reserved nodes.
[04:20] Asha: So we'd either reserve a larger baseline or rely on burst. We prefer predictable invoices — our CFO hates huge delta bills.
[04:28] Maya: We can do reserved capacity contracts with committed monthly usage to cap costs, plus optional burst capacity billed at a premium. We can model a blended effective unit cost.
[04:38] Leo: How fast can reserved nodes prewarm? If we want to spin up N nodes for an expected event announced an hour before, what's the prewarm time?
[04:47] Carlos: Prewarm time varies by model size and infra; typical warm-pool prewarmed containers can be ready in 2–6 minutes, whole-node prewarm may take longer (10–20 minutes) depending on image pull and KV cache sizing. We offer hotpool options that keep a small number of VM instances in memory for near-instant readiness at an extra cost.
[05:05] Asha: The marketing team sometimes gives us a 30-minute heads up; sometimes it's zero. For zero notice, we'd need hotpool or immediate fallback.
[05:14] Maya: Precisely. Hotpool is the recommended option for unpredictable zero-notice surges; it's priced as reserved compute but with a smaller footprint kept in RAM.
[05:22] Jordan: On autoscaling — if we autoscale reserved nodes, is there any chance of preemption? How do you handle reclaim between customers?
[05:29] Carlos: For reserved pools, there is no preemption by other tenants. For dedicated but flexible pools we might reclaim during capacity pressure but only with notice per SLA. Hosted burst capacity is elastic and shared.
[05:39] Leo: Performance: can you share any in-house benchmarks for LlamaX-70B analogs? We care about tokens/sec per GPU and this affects sizing.
[05:47] Carlos: I can share a benchmark sheet after the call; preliminary numbers: 70B quantized on H100 ~ 60–90 tokens/sec single-stream, with effective multi-stream concurrency depending on batching and prefix cache. I will include sample numbers for 16k and 32k contexts.
[06:05] Asha: About batching — we need low tail latency for chat. Large batching helps throughput but hurts p99. How do you balance?
[06:13] Carlos: Runtime uses continuous batching tuned by latency SLO. You can set per-route latency targets — the system will reduce batch window for low-latency routes. Also prefix/KV cache reduces compute for repeated contexts.
[06:25] Jordan: Any multitenant noisy neighbor mitigation aside from whole-node? We've seen cgroups leak GPU memory before.
[06:32] Carlos: We have kernel-level guardrails and runtime-level quota enforcement. But for strict workloads we recommend whole-node pinning.
[06:38] Maya: Quick interruption — Asha, you mentioned batch embedding jobs overnight. Would you consider isolated spot-like cheaper nodes for batch?
[06:46] Asha: Yes, embed jobs are cost-sensitive and can run on preemptible or cheaper zones; not mission-critical. But they must not interfere with daytime chat pools.
[06:55] Carlos: That's a classic pattern: dedicated low-cost pool for offline jobs and reserved pool for real-time. We can also schedule maintenance windows to avoid conflicts.
[07:04] Leo: On the security front, we need to know where data rests. For Dedicated, is data stored on Redwood-managed storage or pushed to our GCS buckets?
[07:12] Carlos: For Dedicated managed instances, model weights and ephemeral caches are on Redwood-provisioned storage, but we support mounting customer-managed buckets for persistent artifacts on Private deployments. For strict data residency we recommend Private or on-prem.
[07:26] Jordan: If we go Private (VPC/on-prem), what's the deployment effort and timeline?
[07:31] Maya: Private deployments take longer: initial setup 6–10 weeks typical, depends on your infra and approvals. We provide an on-prem package and assist with onboarding. Dedicated managed can be turned on faster — days to weeks depending on contractual approvals.
[07:45] Asha: Our timeline — we need a pilot within 8 weeks and GA in 5 months. Budget cycles end next quarter so cost predictability is big.
[07:55] Maya: That timeline is doable. Pilot on a subset of traffic using Dedicated nodes with a small hotpool for spikes, then expand.
[08:02] Carlos: Operationally, we'll want runbooks: escalation matrix, playbook for surge, and fallback policies. I can share our burst playbook.
[08:10] Maya: We'll send a recommended architecture diagram — numbers included, like nodes, expected QPS, and cost estimates.
[08:16] Asha: Can you do a trial? We might want a 2-week pilot with a small reserved pool to test latency and isolation.
[08:23] Maya: Yes, we often do pilot reservations. It helps validate perf and ops assumptions. We'll need a statement of work for reserved capacity.
[08:30] Leo: Operational question — how do you handle logs and PII redaction? We prefer no raw transcripts to leave our VPC.
[08:37] Carlos: You can configure redact rules; logs can be pushed to your SIEM without sensitive fields. For higher assurance, use Private deployment and keep logs internal.
[08:46] Jordan: Anything about patching and maintenance windows that will impact availability?
[08:51] Carlos: We have rolling upgrades and scheduled maintenance with SLA-provided notice windows. For enterprise, you can set maintenance blackout windows.
[08:59] Asha: Pricing: will you give an estimate for reserved monthly cost vs burst unit price? We need a blended model for forecasting.
[09:07] Maya: We'll provide a pricing scenario: committed capacity cost, hotpool add-on, and burst rate (per token at premium). We'll model three scenarios: conservative reserve, medium reserve + burst, and minimal reserve + large burst.
[09:22] Leo: Another technical thing — do you support GPU types? We prefer H100 for perf but A100 may be cheaper. Can we specify hardware?
[09:31] Carlos: Yes, you can request hardware preferences; availability varies by region. We can show performance/cost trade-offs for A100 vs H100. Some customers mix: H100 for low-latency real-time, A100 for batch.
[09:43] Jordan: If we commit to a contract, what's the SLA for latency and time to recovery?
[09:49] Maya: SLA terms are negotiable on enterprise contracts. Standard is uptime with credits; latency SLOs are operational targets. We can attach guaranteed isolation and prioritized capacity for a contractual fee.
[10:02] Asha: Any limits on connection counts or per-tenant quotas?
[10:07] Carlos: You can set per-tenant and per-route quotas; console enforces quotas and rate-limits.
[10:12] Leo: How's the telemetry surfaced? We need token-level breakdown and p99 latency per route.
[10:17] Maya: Console exposes token and cost breakdowns, per-model and per-route dashboards. We can also stream metrics to your Datadog.
[10:24] Jordan: Ok, let's talk about a concrete pilot config. Suppose we reserve 4 nodes H100-class, a hotpool of 2 prewarmed containers, and keep a hosted burst allowance. What's the expected headroom for a 3k concurrent spike?
[10:35] Carlos: Very rough: 4 H100 nodes + 2 hotpool instances might handle ~600–800 conc with low p99; to reach 3k you'd rely heavily on hosted fallback or prewarm additional nodes. A more conservative reserved base (8–10 nodes) would cover spikes but costs more. We'll put precise numbers in the calc.
[10:53] Maya: We'll produce a model showing cost vs percent on-hosted vs dedicated. That will help your finance.
[10:59] Asha: Onboard gating: who needs to sign off internally? Security team, infra, and procurement. We'll likely start procurement after pilot results.
[11:07] Maya: Understood — we can coordinate with your procurement. We'll include SOC2, penetration test summary, and contract terms.
[11:13] Leo: Quick question about tokenization differences between our current stack and Redwood runtime. Will we see token accounting differences?
[11:20] Carlos: There can be small differences across tokenizers; we provide token accounting and will help reconcile meters.
[11:26] Jordan: If we need to run legal review, how long does that typically take?
[11:30] Maya: Legal cycles vary; for enterprise it can be 2–6 weeks. We provide a standard addendum for data handling and can fast-track with your procurement.
[11:38] Asha: Great. Anything else on compliance? Data residency: we need EU and NA region support.
[11:43] Maya: We have region-locked deployments for EU and NA. For strict residency, Private is recommended.
[11:49] Leo: Are there limits to context window? We plan to use 32k.
[11:53] Carlos: We support large contexts; performance will vary by model and hardware. We'll include perf for 32k in the bench sheet.
[11:59] Asha: Cool. Can you also include failure-mode playbooks — e.g., if a node goes down mid-spike, how do we gracefully degrade?
[12:06] Carlos: Yes, we'll include a failover plan: route to hotpool, degrade quality, or fall back to hosted, with circuit breaker to protect origin.
[12:16] Maya: Recap and next steps: we'll send the pricing scenarios, burst playbook, proposed pilot SOW, and benchmark sheet. Carlos will prepare perf numbers and topology diagram. Penumbra to share traffic histograms and SLOs.
[12:31] Asha: Sounds good. We'll schedule the technical deep dive next week; Jordan and Leo will attend.
[12:36] Maya: Great. Thanks everyone.

Post-call notes (auto-generated):
- Customer most interested in predictable cost and tenant isolation with burst safety mechanisms.
- Pilot recommended: 4-node reserved H100 pool + 2-instance hotpool; measure p50/p95/p99 for chat flows and stress tests to simulate 3k conc.
- Risks: zero-notice spikes may require significant hotpool or hosted burst; PII policy may disallow hosted fallback for sensitive traffic.
